text: William Franklin Graham Jr. (/ˈɡreɪəm/; November 7, 1918 – February 21, 2018) was an American evangelist, ordained Southern Baptist minister, and civil rights advocate whose broadcasts and world tours featuring live sermons became well known in the mid-to-late 20th century. Over a career spanning more than six decades, Graham rose to prominence as an evangelical Christian figure in the United States and abroad. According to a biographer, he was considered "among the most influential Christian leaders" of the 20th century. Beginning in the late 1940s and early 1950s, Graham became known for filling stadiums and other massive venues around the world where he preached live sermons, which were often broadcast via radio and television, with some continuing into the 21st century. He hosted his annual "crusades," evangelistic live-campaigns, from 1947 until his retirement in 2005, and hosted the radio show *Hour of Decision* from 1950 to 1954. He repudiated racial segregation, insisting on racial integration for all of his revivals and crusades as early as 1953, and later invited Martin Luther King Jr. to preach jointly at a revival in New York City in 1957. He helped shape the worldview of a large number of people from diverse backgrounds, leading them to find a relationship between the Bible and contemporary secular viewpoints. According to his website, Graham spoke to live audiences of at least 210 million people in more than 185 countries and territories through various meetings, including BMS World Mission and Global Mission events. Graham was close to U.S. presidents Dwight D. Eisenhower, Lyndon B. Johnson (one of his closest friends), and Richard Nixon. He was also a lifelong friend with Robert Schuller, another televangelist and founding pastor of the Crystal Cathedral, whom Graham encouraged to start his own television ministry. Graham was appreciated by mainline Protestant denominations, as he encouraged mainline Protestants converted to his evangelical message to remain within or return to their mainline churches. Despite early suspicions toward Catholicism common among evangelical Protestants, Graham eventually developed amicable ties with many American Catholic Church figures and later encouraged unity between Catholics and Protestants. Graham operated a variety of media and publishing outlets; according to his staff, more than 3.2 million people responded to the invitation at Billy Graham Crusades to "accept Jesus Christ as their personal savior." His lifetime audience, including radio and television broadcasts, likely surpassed billions of people. As a result of his crusades, Graham preached the gospel to more people, live and in-person, than anyone in the history of Christianity. He was on Gallup's list of most admired men and women a record 61 times. Grant Wacker wrote that by the mid-1960s, he had become the "Great Legitimator," saying: "By then his presence conferred status on presidents, acceptability on wars, shame on racial prejudice, desirability on decency, dishonor on indecency, and prestige on civic events." Graham was born on November 7, 1918, in the downstairs bedroom of a farmhouse near Charlotte, North Carolina. Of Scots-Irish descent, he was the eldest of four children born to Morrow (née Coffey) and dairy farmer William Franklin Graham Sr. He was raised on the family dairy farm with his two younger sisters Catherine Morrow and Jean and younger brother Melvin Thomas. When he was nine, the family moved about 75 yards (69 m) from their white frame house to a newly built red brick house. He was raised by his parents in the Associate Reformed Presbyterian Church. Graham attended the Sharon Grammar School and started reading books early, especially novels for boys like Tarzan, which inspired him to hang on trees and give the Tarzan yell; according to his father, this yelling led him to become a minister. Graham was 15 when Prohibition ended in December 1933, and his father forced him and his sister Catherine to drink beer until they became sick, creating a lifelong aversion to alcohol and drugs. Graham was turned down for membership in a local youth group for being "too worldly." Albert McMakin, who worked on the Graham farm, persuaded him to see evangelist Mordecai Ham. According to his autobiography, Graham was 16 when he was converted during a series of revival meetings that Ham led in Charlotte in 1934. After graduating from Sharon High School in May 1936, Graham attended Bob Jones College, where he found the coursework and rules too legalistic and was almost expelled, but Bob Jones Sr. warned him not to throw his life away, saying, "At best, all you could amount to would be a poor country Baptist preacher somewhere out in the sticks... You have a voice that pulls. God can use that voice of yours. He can use it mightily." In 1937, Graham transferred to the Florida Bible Institute in Temple Terrace, Florida. While still a student, he preached his first sermon at Bostwick Baptist Church near Palatka, Florida. In his autobiography, he wrote of receiving his calling on the 18th green of the Temple Terrace Golf and Country Club, adjacent to the institute's campus. Reverend Billy Graham Memorial Park was later established on the Hillsborough River, directly east of the 18th green and across from where Graham often paddled a canoe to a small island in the river, where he would practice preaching to the birds, alligators, and cypress stumps. In 1939, Graham was ordained by a group of Southern Baptist clergy at Peniel Baptist Church in Palatka, Florida. In 1940, he graduated with a Bachelor of Theology degree. Graham then enrolled at Wheaton College in Wheaton, Illinois, where he decided to accept the Bible as the infallible word of God. Henrietta Mears of the First Presbyterian Church of Hollywood in California helped him wrestle with this issue, which he settled at Forest Home Christian Camp (now called Forest Home Ministries) southeast of Big Bear Lake in southern California. While attending Wheaton, Graham was invited to preach one Sunday in 1941 at the United Gospel Tabernacle church. After that, the congregation repeatedly asked him to preach at their church and later asked him to become its pastor. After praying and seeking advice from his friend Dr. Edman, Graham became their church's pastor. In June 1943, Graham graduated from Wheaton College with a degree in anthropology. That same year, Robert Van Kampen, treasurer of the National Gideon Association, invited Graham to preach at Western Springs Baptist Church, and Graham accepted the opportunity on the spot. While there, his friend Torrey Johnson, pastor of the Midwest Bible Church in Chicago, told Graham that his radio program, *Songs in the Night*, was about to be canceled due to lack of funding. Consulting with members of his church in Western Springs, Graham decided to take over Johnson's program with financial support from his congregation. Launching the new radio program on January 2, 1944, still called *Songs in the Night*, Graham recruited the bass-baritone George Beverly Shea as his director of radio ministry. With World War II underway, Graham applied to become a chaplain in the U.S. Army. After being initially turned down for being underweight, he was awarded a commission as a Second Lieutenant but came down with a severe case of mumps in October 1944 before beginning chaplain training at Harvard Divinity School and was bedridden for six weeks. Due to his illness and the expectation that the war would end soon, he was discharged from the army. After a period of recuperation in Florida, he was hired as the first full-time evangelist of the new Youth for Christ (YFC), co-founded by Torrey Johnson and Canadian evangelist Charles Templeton. In his first year as a YFC evangelist, Graham spoke in 47 U.S. states. He traveled extensively as an evangelist in the United States and Europe in the immediate post-war era, making his first overseas trip in 1946. In 1948, in a Modesto, California hotel room, Graham and his evangelistic team established the Modesto Manifesto: a code of ethics for life and work to protect against accusations of financial, sexual, and power abuse. The code includes rules for collecting offerings in churches, working only with churches supportive of cooperative evangelism, using official crowd estimates at outdoor events, and a commitment to never be alone with a woman other than his wife (which became known as the "Billy Graham rule"). Graham was 29 when he became president of Northwestern Bible College in Minneapolis in 1948, making him the youngest president of a college or university in the country, and held the position for four years before resigning in 1952. While serving in this position, Charles Templeton urged him to apply to Princeton Theological Seminary for an advanced theological degree after he himself had done so, but Graham declined and continued as president. The first Billy Graham Crusade was held on September 13–21, 1947, at the Civic Auditorium in Grand Rapids, Michigan, and was attended by 6,000 people. Graham was 28 years old then, and would rent a large venue (such as a stadium, park, or even a street); as crowds grew, he arranged for a group of up to 5,000 people to sing in a choir. He would preach the gospel and invite individuals to come forward (a practice begun by Dwight L. Moody); such people were called "inquirers" and were given the chance to speak one-on-one with a counselor to clarify questions and pray together. The inquirers were often given a copy of the Gospel of John or a Bible study booklet. In 1949, Graham scheduled a series of revival meetings in Los Angeles, for which he erected circus tents in a parking lot. He attracted national media coverage, especially in the conservative Hearst chain of newspapers, although Hearst and Graham never met. The crusade event ran for eight weeks—five weeks longer than originally planned. Graham became a national figure, with heavy coverage from the wire services and national magazines. Pianist Rudy Atwood, who played for the tent meetings, wrote that they "rocketed Billy Graham into national prominence, and resulted in the conversion of a number of show-business personalities." In 1953, Graham was offered a five-year, $1 million contract from NBC to appear on television opposite Arthur Godfrey, but he had prior commitments and turned down the offer to continue his live touring revivals. Graham held crusades in London that lasted 12 weeks, and a New York City crusade at Madison Square Garden in 1957, which ran nightly for 16 weeks. At a 1973 rally in Durban, South Africa—the first large mixed-race event in apartheid South Africa—Graham openly declared that "apartheid is a sin." In Moscow, Russia, in 1992, one-quarter of the 155,000 people in Graham's audience went forward at his call. During his crusades, he frequently used the altar call song, "Just As I Am." In 1995, during the Global Mission event, he preached a sermon at Estadio Hiram Bithorn in San Juan, Puerto Rico, that was transmitted by satellite to 185 countries and translated into 116 languages. By the time of his last crusade in 2005 in New York City, he had preached 417 live crusades, including 226 in the U.S. and 195 abroad. Graham spoke at InterVarsity Christian Fellowship's Urbana Student Missions Conference at least nine times—in 1948, 1957, 1961, 1964, 1976, 1979, 1981, 1984, and 1987. At each Urbana conference, he challenged the thousands of attendees to make a commitment to follow Jesus Christ for the rest of their lives. He often quoted a six-word phrase reportedly written in the Bible of William Whiting Borden, the son of a wealthy silver magnate: "No reserves, no retreat, no regrets." Borden had died in Egypt on his way to the mission field. Graham also held evangelistic meetings on several college campuses: at the University of Minnesota during InterVarsity's "Year of Evangelism" in 1950–51, a 4-day mission at Yale University in 1957, and a week-long series of meetings at the University of North Carolina's Carmichael Auditorium in September 1982. In 1955, he was invited by Cambridge University students to lead the mission at the university; the mission was arranged by the Cambridge Inter-Collegiate Christian Union, with London pastor-theologian John Stott serving as Graham's chief assistant. This invitation was greeted with much disapproval in the correspondence columns of *The Times*. In 1950, Graham founded the Billy Graham Evangelistic Association (BGEA) with its headquarters in Minneapolis. The association relocated to Charlotte, North Carolina, in 2003, and maintains a number of international offices, such as in Hong Kong, Tokyo, and Buenos Aires. BGEA ministries have included: In April 2013, the Billy Graham Evangelistic Association started "My Hope With Billy Graham," the largest outreach in its history. It encouraged church members to spread the gospel in small group meetings after showing a video message by Graham. "The idea is for Christians to follow the example of the disciple Matthew in the New Testament and spread the gospel in their own homes." "The Cross" video is the main program in the My Hope America series and was also broadcast the week of Graham's 95th birthday. Graham's early crusades were segregated, but he began adjusting his approach in the 1950s. During a 1953 rally in Chattanooga, Tennessee, Graham tore down the ropes that organizers had erected to segregate the audience into racial sections. In his memoirs, he recounted that he told two ushers to leave the barriers down "or you can go on and have the revival without me." During a sermon held at Vanderbilt University in Nashville on August 23, 1954, he warned a white audience, "Three-fifths of the world is not white. They are rising all over the world. We have been proud and thought we were better than any other race, any other people. Ladies and gentlemen, I want to tell you that we are going to stumble into hell because of our pride." In 1957, Graham's stance toward integration became more publicly visible when he allowed black ministers Thomas Kilgore and Gardner C. Taylor to serve as members of his New York Crusade's executive committee. He also invited Martin Luther King Jr., whom he first met during the Montgomery bus boycott in 1955, to join him in the pulpit at his 16-week revival in New York City, where 2.3 million gathered at Madison Square Garden, Yankee Stadium, and Times Square to hear them. Graham recalled in his autobiography that during this time, he and King developed a close friendship and that he was eventually one of the few people who referred to King as "Mike," a nickname which King asked only his closest friends to call him. Following King's assassination in 1968, Graham mourned that the U.S. had lost "a social leader and a prophet." In private, Graham advised King and other members of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC). Despite their friendship, tensions between Graham and King emerged in 1958, when the sponsoring committee of a crusade that took place in San Antonio, Texas, on July 25 arranged for Graham to be introduced by that state's segregationist governor, Price Daniel. On July 23, King sent a letter to Graham and informed him that allowing Daniel to speak at a crusade that occurred the night before the state's Democratic Primary "can well be interpreted as your endorsement of racial segregation and discrimination." Graham's advisor, Grady Wilson, replied to King that "even though we do not see eye to eye with him on every issue, we still love him in Christ." Though Graham's appearance with Daniel dashed King's hopes of holding joint crusades with Graham in the Deep South, the two remained friends; the next year King told a Canadian television audience that Graham had taken a "very strong stance against segregation." Graham and King would also come to differ on the Vietnam War. After King's "Beyond Vietnam" speech denouncing U.S. intervention in Vietnam, Graham castigated him and others for their criticism of U.S. foreign policy. By the middle of 1960, King and Graham traveled together to the Tenth Baptist World Congress of the Baptist World Alliance. In 1963, Graham posted bail for King to be released from jail during the Birmingham (Alabama) campaign, according to Michael Long, and the King Center acknowledged that Graham had bailed King out of jail during the Albany Movement.

At a crusade held the night before the state's Democratic Primary, King was criticized for what was described as an endorsement of racial segregation and discrimination. Graham's advisor, Grady Wilson, responded to King by stating, "even though we do not see eye to eye with him on every issue, we still love him in Christ." Although Graham's appearance with Daniel undermined King's hopes of joint crusades in the Deep South, the two remained friends; the following year, King told a Canadian television audience that Graham had taken a "very strong stance against segregation." The two also disagreed on the Vietnam War, as after King delivered his "Beyond Vietnam" speech criticizing U.S. involvement, Graham condemned him and others for their criticism of U.S. foreign policy. By mid-1960, King and Graham traveled together to the Tenth Baptist World Congress of the Baptist World Alliance. In 1963, Graham posted bail for King during the Birmingham (Alabama) campaign, according to Michael Long, and the King Center confirmed that Graham had bailed King out of jail during the Albany Movement, though historian Steven Miller could not verify the incident. Graham held integrated crusades in Birmingham on Easter 1964, following the bombing of the Sixteenth Street Baptist Church, and toured Alabama after the violence during the first Selma to Montgomery march in 1965. After Graham's death, former SCLC official Andrew Young, who spoke alongside Coretta Scott King at Graham's 1994 crusade in Atlanta, acknowledged their friendship and stated that Graham had traveled with King to the 1965 European Baptist Convention. Young also said Graham often invited King to his Northern crusades. Former SNCC leader John Lewis credited Graham as a major inspiration for his activism, describing him as a "saint" who "taught us how to live and who taught us how to die." Graham's faith led him to develop a mature view of race and segregation; he told a Ku Klux Klan member that integration was necessary for religious reasons, asserting, "There is no scriptural basis for segregation," and adding, "The ground at the foot of the cross is level, and it touches my heart when I see whites standing shoulder to shoulder with blacks at the cross." His friendship with John Stott led to a partnership in the Lausanne Movement, stemming from Graham's 1966 World Congress on Evangelism in Berlin. In collaboration with Christianity Today, Graham convened the International Congress on World Evangelization in Lausanne, Switzerland (July 16–25, 1974), which gathered 2,700 participants from 150 nations; women were represented by Millie Dienert, who chaired the prayer committee. The movement, named after the host city, aimed to strengthen the global church for world evangelization and engage ideological and sociological trends. Graham invited Stott to be chief architect of the Lausanne Covenant, which he said "helped challenge and unite evangelical Christians in the great task of world evangelization." The movement remains a significant part of Graham's legacy, present in nearly every nation. Graham played multiple roles that reinforced each other: preacher, icon, Southerner, entrepreneur, architect (bridge builder), pilgrim, pastor, and America's Protestant patriarch, comparable to Martin Luther King and Pope John Paul II. He served as a trustee of the International Mission Board in the late 1950s and of the SBC's Radio and Television Commission in the late 1960s. As a bridge builder, Graham deliberately engaged the secular world, such as by building his own pavilion for the 1964 New York World's Fair and appearing on a 1969 Woody Allen television special. During the Cold War, he became the first evangelist to speak behind the Iron Curtain, addressing large crowds in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union for peace. During the apartheid era, he refused to visit South Africa until its government allowed integrated seating; during his 1973 crusade there, he openly denounced apartheid and corresponded with imprisoned Nelson Mandela. In 1984, he led Mission England in the United Kingdom, using outdoor football (soccer) fields as venues. Graham promoted global evangelism by sponsoring training conferences in 1983, 1986, and 2000, with over 157 nations gathering in 2000 at the RAI Convention Center in Amsterdam. At a revival in Seoul, South Korea, he attracted more than one million people. He appeared in China in 1988, a homecoming for his wife Ruth, born in China to missionary parents, and in North Korea in 1992. On October 15, 1989, he received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, the only minister to do so in that capacity. On September 22, 1991, he held his largest North American event on the Great Lawn of Manhattan's Central Park, with over 250,000 attendees estimated. In 1998, he spoke to scientists and philosophers at the Technology, Entertainment, Design Conference. On September 14, 2001, three days after the World Trade Center attacks, he led a service at Washington National Cathedral attended by President George W. Bush and past and present leaders, and he also spoke at the memorial service for the Oklahoma City bombing in 1995. From June 24–26, 2005, he began what he said would be his last North American crusade at Flushing Meadows–Corona Park in Queens, New York City. On March 11–12, 2006, he held the "Festival of Hope" with his son Franklin in New Orleans, which was recovering from Hurricane Katrina. He prepared a final sermon, "My Hope America," released on DVD and played across America and possibly worldwide between November 7–10, 2013, with November 7 being his 95th birthday and his hope for a revival. Graham stated his planned retirement was due to failing health, specifically hydrocephalus since 1992. In August 2005, he appeared at the groundbreaking for his library in Charlotte, North Carolina, then 86, using a walker. On July 9, 2006, he spoke at the Metro Maryland Franklin Graham Festival in Baltimore, Maryland, at Oriole Park at Camden Yards. In April 2010, at age 91 and experiencing vision, hearing, and balance loss, he made a rare public appearance at the re-dedication of the renovated Billy Graham Library. There was family controversy over his burial place; in June 2007, he announced he and his wife would be buried at the Billy Graham Library in Charlotte. His younger son Ned argued with older son Franklin over burial at a library, and Ruth Graham had expressed a desire to be buried in the mountains at the Billy Graham Training Center at The Cove near Asheville, North Carolina, where she had lived; Ned supported her choice. Novelist Patricia Cornwell opposed burial at the library, calling it a tourist attraction. Franklin wanted his parents buried at the library site. When Ruth Graham died, it was announced they would be buried at the library. In 2011, when asked if he would have done things differently, he said he would have spent more time at home with his family, studied more, preached less, and participated in fewer conferences, also noting a habit of advising evangelists to avoid too many commitments. After close relationships with Lyndon B. Johnson and Richard Nixon, Graham avoided explicit partisanship, declining to sign or endorse political statements and distancing himself from the Christian right. His early opposition to communism evolved into calls for military disarmament and attention to AIDS, poverty, and environmental threats. Graham was a lifelong registered member of the Democratic Party. In 1960, he opposed John F. Kennedy, fearing a Catholic president would follow the Pope, and worked behind the scenes to encourage Protestant ministers to oppose Kennedy. He met with a Protestant ministers' conference in Montreux, Switzerland, to mobilize congregations against Kennedy, and organized a meeting of hundreds of Protestant ministers in Washington, D.C. in September 1960, led by Norman Vincent Peale. This occurred shortly before Kennedy's speech in Houston on the separation of church and state, which was successful in addressing voter concerns. After Kennedy's election, he invited Graham to play golf in Palm Beach, Florida, after which Graham acknowledged the election as an opportunity for Catholics and Protestants to unite. The two remained in touch, meeting last at a National Day of Prayer in February 1963. In his autobiography, Graham claimed to have felt an "inner foreboding" the week before Kennedy's assassination and tried to contact him to say, "Don't go to Texas!" Graham opposed most abortions but supported them in narrow circumstances: rape, incest, and when the mother's life was at risk. The Billy Graham Evangelistic Association states, "Life is sacred, and we must seek to protect all human life: the unborn, the child, the adult, and the aged." Graham leaned toward Republicans during Richard Nixon's presidency, whom he had met and befriended as vice president under Dwight D. Eisenhower. He did not fully align with the religious right, stating that Jesus did not have a political party. He supported various political candidates over the years. In 2007, he explained his refusal to join Jerry Falwell's Moral Majority in 1979, saying, "I'm for morality, but morality goes beyond sex to human freedom and social justice. We as clergy know so very little to speak with authority on the Panama Canal or superiority of armaments. Evangelists cannot be closely identified with any particular party or person. We have to stand in the middle to preach to all people, right and left. I haven't been faithful to my own advice in the past. I will be in the future." In a 2006 Newsweek interview, Graham said politics was secondary to the Gospel, and when asked whether ministers should engage in politics, he replied, "You know, I think in a way that has to be up to the individual as he feels led of the Lord. A lot of things that I commented on years ago would not have been of the Lord, I'm sure, but I think you have some – like communism, or segregation, on which I think you have a responsibility to speak out." In 2011, although grateful to have met politicians with spiritual needs, he said he sometimes crossed the line and would have preferred to avoid politics. In 2012, Graham endorsed Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney; shortly after, to accommodate Romney, a Mormon, references to Mormonism as a "cult" were removed from Graham's website. Observers questioned whether his support for Republican and religious right positions on issues like same-sex marriage, which came after he stopped speaking publicly, reflected his son Franklin's views. Franklin denied this, stating he would continue to act as his father's spokesperson rather than hold press conferences. In 2016, according to his son Franklin, Graham voted for Donald Trump. This has been disputed by other children and grandchildren, who argue he was too ill to vote and emphasize that Graham's greatest regret in life was becoming involved in partisan politics. Graham had personal audiences with 12 consecutive U.S. presidents, from Harry S. Truman to Barack Obama. After meeting Truman in 1950, Graham urged him to counter communism in North Korea; Truman disliked him and did not speak with him for years. Later, Graham treated all conversations with presidents as confidential. Truman publicly criticized Graham in his 1974 autobiography, calling him a "counterfeit" and saying he was only interested in getting his name in the paper. Graham urged Dwight D. Eisenhower to intervene with federal troops to allow the Little Rock Nine to attend public schools. House Speaker Sam Rayburn allowed Graham to conduct the first religious service on the steps of the Capitol in 1952. Eisenhower asked for Graham while on his deathbed. Graham became a close friend of Vice President Richard Nixon and supported Nixon, a Quaker, in the 1960 election. He convened an August 1960 strategy session in Montreux, Switzerland, to plan opposition to Nixon's Catholic opponent, Senator John F. Kennedy. Though a registered Democrat, Graham strongly supported anti-communism and sympathized with Nixon's foreign policy views, thus being more sympathetic to Republican administrations. On December 16, 1963, President Lyndon B. Johnson, impressed by Graham's praise of his great-grandfather George Washington Baines, invited Graham to the White House for spiritual counseling. After this visit, Johnson frequently called on Graham for spiritual counseling and companionship. Graham recalled, "I almost used the White House as a hotel when Johnson was President. He was always trying to keep me there. He just never wanted me to leave." Unlike his limited access with Truman, Eisenhower, and Kennedy, Graham visited Johnson's private quarters and at times knelt at his bedside to pray. Johnson was the first sitting president to attend one of Graham's crusades in Houston, Texas, in 1965. During the 1964 U.S. presidential election, supporters of Barry Goldwater sent an estimated 2 million telegrams to Graham's hometown of Montreat, North Carolina, seeking his endorsement. Graham, supportive of Johnson's domestic policies and wishing to preserve his friendship with the president, resisted pressure to endorse Goldwater and remained neutral. After Johnson's election, Graham's role as the main White House pastor was solidified. Johnson even considered making Graham a cabinet member and grooming him as his successor, though Graham insisted on no political ambitions and wished to remain a preacher. Graham's biographer David Aikman acknowledged that Graham was closer to Johnson than any other president he had known. In February 2025, the BGEA stated that Graham was "probably closer to Johnson than to any other president." He spent the last night of Johnson's presidency in the White House and stayed for the first night of Nixon's. After Nixon's 1968 victory, Graham remained active in public life.

During the 1964 United States presidential election, supporters of Republican nominee Barry Goldwater sent an estimated 2 million telegrams to Graham's hometown of Montreat, North Carolina, seeking his endorsement. Supportive of President Lyndon B. Johnson's domestic policies and wishing to preserve his friendship with the president, Graham resisted pressure to endorse Goldwater and remained neutral. Following Johnson's election victory, Graham's role as the main White House pastor was solidified; Johnson even considered making Graham a cabinet member and grooming him as his successor, though Graham insisted he had no political ambitions and wished to remain a preacher. Graham's biographer David Aikman acknowledged that the preacher was closer to Johnson than any other president he had ever known, and in February 2025, the BGEA stated that Graham was "probably closer to Johnson than to any other president." He spent the last night of Johnson's presidency in the White House and stayed for the first night of Nixon's. After Nixon's 1968 presidential campaign victory, Graham became an adviser, regularly visiting the White House and leading the president's private worship services. In a meeting with Golda Meir, Nixon offered Graham the ambassadorship to Israel, which he declined. In 1970, Nixon appeared at a Graham revival in East Tennessee, which drew one of the largest crowds in Tennessee of Vietnam War protesters; Nixon was the first president to give a speech from an evangelist's platform. Their friendship strained in 1973 when Graham rebuked Nixon for his post-Watergate behavior and the profanity heard on the Watergate tapes; they reconciled after Nixon's resignation. Graham officiated at one presidential burial and one presidential funeral: he presided over the graveside services of President Lyndon B. Johnson in 1973 and participated in eulogizing him; he officiated at the funeral of former First Lady Pat Nixon in 1993 and at the death and state funeral of Richard Nixon in 1994. During the Monica Lewinsky scandal, Graham asserted that he believed President Bill Clinton to be "a spiritual person." He was unable to attend the state funeral of Ronald Reagan on June 11, 2004, due to recovering from hip replacement surgery, a fact mentioned by George W. Bush in his eulogy. On April 25, 2010, President Barack Obama visited Graham at his home in Montreat, North Carolina, where they "had a private prayer." Graham had a friendly relationship with Queen Elizabeth II, first meeting in 1955 and preaching at Windsor Chapel the following year; their relationship may have stemmed from shared traditional views on Christian faith. Graham was outspoken against communism and supported American Cold War policies, including the Vietnam War; in a secret letter from April 15, 1969, made public twenty years later, Graham encouraged Nixon to bomb the dikes in North Vietnam if peace talks in Paris failed, stating the action would "destroy the economy of North Vietnam" and, by Nixon's estimate, would have killed a million people. In 1982, Graham preached in the Soviet Union and attended a wreath-laying ceremony honoring the war dead of World War II, when the Soviets were American allies against Nazism; he voiced fear of a second holocaust, not against Jews, but "a nuclear holocaust," and advised that "our greatest contribution to world peace is to live with Christ every day." In a 1999 speech, Graham discussed his relationship with North Korean leader Kim Il Sung, praising him as a "different kind of communist" and "one of the great fighters for freedom in his country against the Japanese," noting he had never met Kim Jong Il but had "exchanged gifts with him." During the Watergate affair, there were suggestions that Graham had expressed antisemitic opinions in private discussions with Nixon; he denied this, emphasizing his efforts to build bridges with the Jewish community. In 2002, declassified Nixon tapes confirmed that in a 1972 conversation with Nixon, Graham agreed that Jews controlled the American media, calling it a "stranglehold," and suggested that if Nixon was re-elected, they might be able to do something about it. When the tapes were made public, Graham apologized and said, "Although I have no memory of the occasion, I deeply regret comments I apparently made in an Oval Office conversation with President Nixon ... some 30 years ago. ... They do not reflect my views and I sincerely apologize for any offense caused by the remarks." According to Newsweek, the revelation was magnified due to Graham's longstanding support of Israel and his refusal to join calls for Jewish conversion. In 2009, more Nixon tapes were released, in which Graham is heard in a 1973 conversation with Nixon referring to a group of Jewish journalists as "the synagogue of Satan"; a Graham spokesman stated he has never been an antisemite and that the comparison, in line with the Book of Revelation, was directed at those claiming to be Jews but not holding traditional Jewish values. After a 1957 crusade in New York, some fundamentalist Protestant Christians criticized Graham for his ecumenism, even calling him "Antichrist." Graham expressed inclusivist views, stating in a 1997 interview with Robert Schuller that people without explicit faith in Jesus can be saved, as they are members of the body of Christ because they have been called by God, and that they may not know the name of Jesus but know in their hearts they need something they do not have and turn to the only light they have. Iain Murray, from a conservative Protestant perspective, argued that "Graham's concessions are sad words from one who once spoke on the basis of biblical certainties." In 1970, Graham stated that feminism was "an echo of our overall philosophy of permissiveness" and that women did not want to be "competitive juggernauts pitted against male chauvinists," asserting that the role of wife, mother, and homemaker was the destiny of "real womanhood" according to the Judeo-Christian ethic. These assertions, published in the Ladies' Home Journal, elicited protest letters and were offered as a rebuttal to the establishment of "The New Feminism" section following a sit-in protest at the Journal offices. Graham's daughter Bunny recounted that her father denied her and her sisters higher education, saying, "There was never an idea of a career for us"; she wanted to go to nursing school at Wheaton with a five-year program, but her father said no, with no explanation. She added, "He has forgotten that. Mother has not." Graham's daughter Anne is a Christian minister leading AnGeL Ministries. Graham talked his future wife, Ruth, into abandoning her ambition to evangelize in Tibet in favor of marrying him, stating that doing otherwise would be "to thwart God's obvious will." After agreeing to marry him, Graham cited the Bible for claiming authority over her, saying, "then I'll do the leading and you do the following." According to her obituary, Ruth was active in Christian ministry after marriage, often teaching Sunday School, and all three of Graham's daughters became Christian ministers. Graham regarded homosexuality as a sin and in 1974 described it as "a sinister form of perversion." In 1993, he said that AIDS might be a "judgment" from God, but two weeks later retracted the remark, saying, "I don't believe that, and I don't know why I said it." He opposed same-sex marriage, stating that "I believe the home and marriage is the foundation of our society and must be protected," and his obituary noted he did not want to discuss homosexuality as a political issue. Corky Siemaszko, writing for NBC News, noted that after the 1993 incident, Graham "largely steered clear of the subject." However, in a 1997 appearance on the May 2 episode of 20/20, Graham stated, "I think that the Bible teaches that homosexuality is a sin, but the Bible also teaches that pride is a sin, jealously is a sin, and hate is a sin, evil thoughts are a sin, and so I don't think that homosexuality should be chosen as the overwhelming sin that we are doing today." In 2012, Graham and his son Franklin publicly endorsed North Carolina Amendment 1, a measure to ban same-sex marriage in the state, and condemned President Obama's public support for same-sex marriage later that year. Graham was frequently honored by surveys, including "Greatest Living American," and consistently ranked among the most admired persons in the United States and the world, appearing most frequently on Gallup's list of most admired people. On the day of his death, Graham had been on Gallup's Top 10 "Most Admired Man" list 61 times and held the highest rank of any person since the list began in 1948. In 1967, he was the first Protestant to receive an honorary degree from Belmont Abbey College, a Roman Catholic school. In 1983, he was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by U.S. President Ronald Reagan. Graham received the Big Brother of the Year Award for his work on behalf of children, was cited by the George Washington Carver Memorial Institute for contributions to race relations, received the Templeton Foundation Prize for Progress in Religion, and the Sylvanus Thayer Award for his commitment to "Duty, Honor, Country." The "Billy Graham Children's Health Center" in Asheville is named after and funded by Graham. In 1999, the Gospel Music Association inducted Graham into the Gospel Music Hall of Fame to recognize his contributions to Christian music artists such as Michael W. Smith, dc Talk, Amy Grant, Jars of Clay, and others who performed at the Billy Graham Crusades; he was the first non-musician inducted and helped revitalize interest in hymns and create new favorite songs. Singer Michael W. Smith was active in Billy Graham Crusades and Samaritan's Purse and sang "Just As I Am" in a tribute to Graham at the 44th GMA Dove Awards and at the memorial service honoring Graham at the United States Capitol rotunda on February 28, 2018. In 2000, former First Lady Nancy Reagan presented the Ronald Reagan Freedom Award to Graham. In 2001, Queen Elizabeth II awarded him an honorary knighthood, presented by Sir Christopher Meyer, British Ambassador to the U.S., at the British Embassy in Washington DC on December 6, 2001. A professorial chair is named after him at Samford University, the Billy Graham Professor of Evangelism and Church Growth. His alma mater, Wheaton College, has an archive of his papers at the Billy Graham Center. The Southern Baptist Theological Seminary has the Billy Graham School of Missions, Evangelism and Ministry. Graham received 20 honorary degrees and refused at least that many more. In San Francisco, California, the Bill Graham Civic Auditorium is sometimes erroneously called the "Billy Graham Civic Auditorium" and incorrectly considered to be named in his honor, but it is actually named after rock and roll promoter Bill Graham. On May 31, 2007, the $27 million Billy Graham Library was officially dedicated in Charlotte; former presidents Jimmy Carter, George H. W. Bush, and Bill Clinton appeared to celebrate with Graham. A highway in Charlotte bears Graham's name, as does I-240 near his home in Asheville. As Graham's final crusade approached in 2005, his friend Pat Boone created a song in honor of Graham, co-written and produced with David Pack and Billy Dean, digitally combining studio recordings of various artists into a "'We Are the World'-type" production titled "Thank You Billy Graham"; the song's video was introduced by Bono and included Faith Hill, MxPx, John Ford Coley, John Elefante, Mike Herrera, Michael McDonald, Jeffrey Osborne, LeAnn Rimes, Kenny Rogers, Connie Smith, Michael Tait, and other singers, with brief narration by Larry King; it was directed by Brian Lockwood as a tribute album. In 2013, the album My Hope: Songs Inspired by the Message and Mission of Billy Graham was recorded by Amy Grant, Kari Jobe, Newsboys, Matthew West, tobyMac, and other music artists with new songs to honor Graham during his My Hope America outreach and the publication of his book The Reason for My Hope: Salvation. Other songs written to honor Graham include "Hero of the Faith" by Eddie Carswell of NewSong, which became a hit, "Billy, You're My Hero" by Greg Hitchcock, "Billy Graham" by The Swirling Eddies, "Billy Graham's Bible" by Joe Nichols, "Billy Frank" by Randy Stonehill, and an original song titled "Just as I Am" by Fernando Ortega. The movie Billy: The Early Years officially premiered in theaters on October 10, 2008, less than one month before Graham's 90th birthday; Graham did not comment on the film, but his son Franklin released a critical statement on August 18, 2008, noting that the Billy Graham Evangelistic Association "has not collaborated with nor does it endorse the movie"; Graham's eldest daughter, Gigi, praised the film and was hired as a consultant to help promote it. Graham has received several honorary doctorates. On August 13, 1943, Graham married Wheaton classmate Ruth Bell, whose parents were Presbyterian missionaries in China; her father, L. Nelson Bell, was a general surgeon. Ruth died on June 14, 2007, at age 87. The couple were married for almost 64 years. Graham and his wife had five children: Virginia (Gigi) Leftwich Graham Tchividjian (b. 1945), an inspirational speaker and author; Anne Graham Lotz (b. 1948), leader of AnGeL Ministries; Ruth Graham (b. 1950), founder and president of Ruth Graham & Friends and leader of conferences throughout the U.S. and Canada; Franklin Graham (b. 1952), president and CEO of the Billy Graham Evangelistic Association and president and CEO of international relief organization Samaritan's Purse; and Nelson Edman Graham (b. 1958), a pastor who runs East Gates Ministries International, which distributes Christian literature in China. At the time of his death at age 99 in 2018, Graham was survived by five children, 19 grandchildren (including Tullian Tchividjian and Will Graham), 41 great-grandchildren, and 6 great-great-grandchildren. Billy Graham, the CEO of the Billy Graham Evangelistic Association and president and CEO of international relief organization Samaritan's Purse, was also associated with Nelson Edman Graham (b. 1958), a pastor who leads East Gates Ministries International, which distributes Christian literature in China. At the time of his death at age 99 in 2018, Graham was survived by 5 children, 19 grandchildren (including Tullian Tchividjian and Will Graham), 41 great-grandchildren, and 6 great-great-grandchildren. In 1953, he became a member of the First Baptist Church Dallas, though he never lived in Texas; in 2008, he transferred his membership to the First Baptist Church of Spartanburg, South Carolina, approximately 1.5 hours from his home in Montreat, North Carolina. Graham died of natural causes on February 21, 2018, at his home in Montreat, North Carolina, at the age of 99. On February 28 and March 1, 2018, he became the fourth private citizen in U.S. history to lie in honor at the United States Capitol rotunda in Washington, D.C., making him the first religious leader to receive this honor; during the ceremony, Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell and Speaker of the House Paul Ryan referred to him as "America's pastor," and President Donald Trump called him "an ambassador for Christ"; televangelist Jim Bakker praised Graham as the greatest preacher since Jesus and stated that Graham visited him in prison. A private funeral service was held on March 2, 2018, and Graham was buried beside his wife in the Prayer Garden on the northeast side of the Billy Graham Library in Charlotte, North Carolina, at the foot of the cross-shaped brick walkway. His pine plywood casket, handcrafted in 2006 by convicted murderers at the Louisiana State Penitentiary, was topped with a wooden cross nailed to it by the prisoners. He is commemorated on the liturgical calendar of the Anglican Church in North America on February 21. On May 16, 2024, a bronze statue of Graham was unveiled in the U.S. Capitol by House Speaker Mike Johnson. Graham's "My Answer" advice column appeared in newspapers for more than 60 years as of 2017. He authored several books, many of which became bestsellers; in the 1970s, *The Jesus Generation* sold 200,000 copies in the first two weeks after publication; *Angels: God's Secret Agents* achieved sales of one million copies within 90 days of release; and *How to Be Born Again* made publishing history with its first printing of 800,000 copies.
